standard.title: Perspectives and Experiences During the Industrial Revolution
standard.description: the different perspectives and experiences of men, women and children during the Industrial Revolution, and their changing way of life
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine the experiences and perspectives of different groups in historical periods (AC9HH8K04, AC9HH8K09). They have not yet applied this skill to the Industrial Revolution context, examined how technological change affected men, women and children differently, or explored the emergence of trade unions as a collective response to industrial conditions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare and contrast the impact of steam, gas and electricity on people's way of life; investigate the changes in working conditions including long hours, low pay and child labour; and identify the growth of trade unions as a response to industrialisation's impacts on the working class.

nodes.label: Class differentiation — how industrialisation affected rich and poor differently
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how industrialisation affected people differently depending on their social class, and compare the experiences of the wealthy and the working poor.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two ways industrialisation improved conditions for wealthy or middle-class people and at least two ways it worsened conditions for the industrial working class.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the benefits for factory owners, merchants and the growing middle class (profit, new goods, consumer products, improved domestic technology); the worsening conditions for industrial workers (factory discipline, long hours, dangerous conditions, low pay, loss of craft autonomy); the new urban poverty — overcrowded slums, disease, polluted water — that contrasted with the prosperity of industrial capitalism; the agricultural worker experience of displacement; explain how the same technological changes produced radically different experiences depending on social position.
wider: Examine the 'two Englands' framing — used by contemporaries including Benjamin Disraeli — as a way of capturing the radical inequality of industrial society
Investigate specific living conditions in an industrial city using census data, social investigations (e.g. Engels' Condition of the Working Class in England) or contemporary journalism
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that industrialisation produced radically different experiences by class is the prerequisite for understanding the differentiated experiences of men, women and children (N2) and the trade union response (N3). Students who do not have this framework will describe industrialisation as uniformly positive or negative rather than as a process of uneven benefit.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe the Industrial Revolution as either a story of progress (for the wealthy) or suffering (for workers) without understanding how the same process produced both simultaneously. Making the class-differentiated experience explicit is the scaffold for the nuanced perspective analysis the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Describes at least two ways industrialisation improved conditions for wealthy or middle-class people
Describes at least two ways it worsened conditions for the industrial working class

nodes.label: Gendered and age-based experiences — men, women and children
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare the different experiences of men, women and children in industrial workplaces and domestic life, and explain how technological change affected each group's way of life.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least one distinct experience of each group (men, women, children) in the industrial context and explain how it differed from pre-industrial experience.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe men's roles in heavy industry, mining, railways — the physical danger, long hours, and how factory discipline transformed working life from craft to machine-paced labour; women's industrial employment — textile mills, domestic service, limited wage levels, the tension between industrial work and domestic responsibilities; children's experiences — as cheap labour in mills, mines and chimneys, the debates about child labour and the Factory Acts; examine how steam, gas and electricity affected domestic life differently for rich and poor households; explain how industrialisation both drew women and children into paid labour and gradually created pressure for their protection from it.
wider: Examine the Parliamentary Select Committee reports and Factory Acts as sources — analysing what the testimony of child workers revealed about conditions and what drove legislative reform

Investigate the contradictions in middle-class attitudes to working-class women and children — the domestic ideal vs economic necessity — and what these contradictions reveal about class and gender values in industrial society
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Parliamentary testimony from child workers and women in industrial employment is historically significant primary source material that provides a direct window into lived experience. It integrates source analysis with content knowledge in a compelling way.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly focus on one group (often children, as the most dramatic case) without building the full differentiated picture across men, women and children. Multiple examples across all three groups are required.

success_criteria: Describes the distinct industrial experience of each of the three groups — men, women and children
Explains how at least one group's experience changed from pre-industrial to industrial conditions

nodes.label: Trade unions — collective response to industrial conditions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the growth of trade unions as a response to industrialisation's impacts on the working class, and explain what problems trade unions addressed and what they achieved.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe trade unions as worker organisations formed to negotiate collectively for wages and conditions, explain what industrial conditions made them necessary, and describe at least one thing they achieved.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the development of trade unions from illegal combinations to recognised organisations; the specific grievances they addressed — long hours, dangerous conditions, child labour, arbitrary dismissal, low wages; early forms of collective action (strikes, mutual aid societies); the legal battles (Combination Acts, their repeal, the Tolpuddle Martyrs); what unions eventually achieved — shorter working hours, improved safety, minimum wage negotiations, political representation through labour parties; explain why collective action was necessary when individual workers had no bargaining power.
wider: Examine the Tolpuddle Martyrs case as a turning point in trade union history — and what it reveals about the balance of power between workers, employers and the state in early industrial Britain
Trace how British trade unionism influenced the Australian labour movement — connecting the Industrial Revolution strand to the Australian Nation strand (AC9HH9K02, K05)

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat trade unions as a given feature of industrial society without understanding why collective organisation was necessary — why individual workers had no bargaining power against employers. Making the power asymmetry explicit is the scaffold for understanding why collective action emerged and what it could achieve.

success_criteria: Describes trade unions as a collective response to industrial conditions and explains what problems they addressed
Explains why collective action was necessary when individual workers lacked bargaining power
